claude_take: Today's stories share one instinct: nobody wants to keep grading their own homework. California just created the country's first outside registry of AI auditors, and Australia is proposing the same logic for social feeds -- letting users opt out of the algorithm instead of trusting platforms to tune it responsibly -- while Meta built its new Muse agent to deliberately sit outside its own ad-targeting system, a design choice that only makes sense if self-policing has stopped being convincing. The DOJ's deeper look at Fox's Roku deal is the same impulse aimed at old-fashioned media concentration rather than algorithms. And when a fragile Yemeni truce and confidence in European luxury houses both crack in the same week, it's a reminder that even outside tech, the referee's credibility -- not the rules on paper -- is what everything else depends on.
claude_take_title: Nobody Wants to Grade Their Own Homework

items.headline: Meta Launches Muse, a Personal AI Agent That Acts on Your Behalf
items.summary: Meta introduced Muse, a personal AI agent that can browse the web, fill out forms, buy movie tickets, and negotiate on a user's behalf, running on its own secure virtual machine that Meta says stays separate from its ad-targeting systems. It's rolling out in the US through a dedicated app, WhatsApp, and the web, with a free tier alongside $20 and $100 monthly plans, for users 18 and older. The launch pushes Meta into the same agentic-AI race as OpenAI and Anthropic, betting that people will trust a Meta product enough to hand over real tasks like shopping and scheduling.

items.headline: California Enacts the Nation's First AI Auditor Registry
items.summary: Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 1405, creating the first state-run registry of independent auditors qualified to inspect AI systems, alongside companion bill SB 813, which sets up a framework for outside verification organizations to check AI systems against state law. Starting January 1, 2029, anyone without a state registration number will be barred from conducting a covered AI audit, ending the practice of AI companies solely grading their own compliance. The bill's author, Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, said the goal is auditors who can identify risks, verify claims, and hold developers to meaningful standards, rather than leaving that entirely to the labs themselves.

items.headline: Fox's $22 Billion Roku Deal Faces Deeper DOJ Antitrust Review
items.summary: The Justice Department issued a formal "second request" for documents in its review of Fox Corp's $22 billion agreement to acquire Roku, extending the legal waiting period until both companies substantially comply. Regulators are examining whether a Fox-owned Roku would give Fox's own channels preferential placement, use Roku's viewer data to boost Fox's advertising business, or push rival streaming apps lower in Roku's interface. Fox still expects the deal, announced in June, to close in the first half of 2027, but the deeper review adds real uncertainty to one of the year's biggest media consolidation bets.

items.headline: US Summer Box Office Officially Closes at an All-Time Record $4.76 Billion
items.summary: The 2026 summer box office finished at $4.76 billion domestically, confirming the record that industry watchers had flagged as likely in late August and topping the prior high-water mark, led by "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" and Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey." The result caps a summer that stayed healthy even with fewer wide releases than pre-pandemic norms, suggesting audiences are turning out for fewer, bigger events rather than a high volume of movies. It's a rare unambiguous win for theatrical exhibition after several years of tempered expectations.

items.headline: Australia Proposes Letting Social Media Users Opt Out of Algorithmic Feeds
items.summary: Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese unveiled a "My Feed, My Way" proposal that would require platforms to let users over 16 choose a chronological feed of only the accounts they follow, instead of an algorithm-curated one, with draft legislation expected to reach Parliament this year. Platforms that fail to notify users of the choice could face fines of up to AU$109.2 million (about US$79 million), and online-safety regulator eSafety would gain new power to force fast removal of harmful or illegal content. It's a separate track from Australia's existing under-16 social media ban, targeting how the algorithm itself shapes what every user sees, not just who can access the platforms at all.

items.headline: Houthi Rebels Seize Yemen's Red Sea Port of Mokha, Threatening a Return to War
items.summary: Iran-backed Houthi forces seized the strategic port city of Mokha on Yemen's Red Sea coast after days of fighting with pro-government forces, their biggest territorial gain since a 2022 truce paused the country's civil war. The advance pushes Houthi control closer to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a chokepoint linking the Red Sea to global shipping and oil markets, raising fears that the fragile truce is effectively over. Pro-government forces have retreated south to Dhubab, adding a new flashpoint to a region already strained by disruptions to Red Sea shipping routes.

items.headline: HSBC Downgrades LVMH and Burberry, Warns of a Tough Second Half for Luxury
items.summary: HSBC cut LVMH and Burberry to "Hold" from "Buy," lowering LVMH's price target to 490 euros and Burberry's to 1,200 pence, citing a tougher run of year-on-year comparisons, softer sentiment in mainland China, and social-media backlash over an intellectual-property dispute involving a Chinese tea brand. Shares in both companies fell more than 2% on the note, which argued investors should take a breather on some luxury stocks until momentum visibly improves. HSBC kept Buy ratings on Richemont, Kering, Moncler, and Prada, suggesting the sector's slowdown is uneven rather than universal.

items.headline: Levinas's Face of the Other
items.headline_fr: Le visage de l'Autre selon Levinas
items.summary: Emmanuel Levinas argued that ethics begins not with abstract rules but with a direct, pre-rational encounter: the "face" of another person, which confronts us with a demand and a vulnerability that precede any reasoning about duty or self-interest. For Levinas, this face resists being reduced to a concept or a category -- it is the Other's irreducible otherness, not our idea of them, that obligates us -- and this responsibility exists prior to and independent of any reciprocity or contract. The idea reframes ethics as fundamentally relational rather than rule-based, and it still shapes contemporary debates over how much moral weight we owe to those we never chose to be responsible for, from refugees to strangers online.
items.summary_fr: Emmanuel Levinas soutient que l'éthique ne commence pas par des règles abstraites, mais par une rencontre directe et pré-rationnelle : le "visage" d'autrui, qui nous impose une exigence et révèle une vulnérabilité antérieures à tout raisonnement sur le devoir ou l'intérêt personnel. Pour Levinas, ce visage résiste à toute réduction à un concept ou à une catégorie -- c'est l'altérité irréductible de l'autre, et non l'idée que nous en avons, qui nous oblige -- et cette responsabilité existe avant et indépendamment de toute réciprocité ou contrat. Cette idée repense l'éthique comme fondamentalement relationnelle plutôt que fondée sur des règles, et elle continue d'irriguer les débats contemporains sur la dette morale que nous devons à ceux envers qui nous n'avons jamais choisi d'être responsables, des réfugiés aux inconnus en ligne.
